newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN urges countries to do more to punish rapists.
newsitem.headline: UN urges countries to do more to punish rapists.

text.p: Women both in the West and in the developing world are being raped, sexually harassed and sold while perpetrators often escape punishment because of legal loopholes, a U.N. special investigator said on Thursday.
The investigator on violence against women, Sri Lankan lawyer Radhika Coomaraswamy, said marriage was also increasingly being used as a method of recruitment for trafficking in women.

"States should amend their penal codes with regard to sexual violence. Sentencing structures should be amended to ensure that perpetrators are duly punished," she said in a report to the annual U.N. Human Rights Commission meeting in Geneva.

In rural China, trading in women under the cover of marriage was so common that between 30 and 90 percent of weddings in some villages resulted from trafficking in women, Coomaraswamy said, quoting statistics from non-governmental organisations.

Statistics showed that more than 5,000 Nigerian women had been sold as wives to farmers in south Italy and nearly 40 percent of some 160,000 Nepalese prostitutes in India had been brought into the country under the pretext of marriage.
Coomaraswamy said university surveys in Canada, Britain and the United States had found as many as 20 percent of female students were rape victims.
But her report was full of sweeping generalisations and failed to give an indepth analysis of key details such as geographical and religious breakdowns of victims and sources.

The report had nearly a full page on one sexual harassment case at the United Nations in 1994. It concluded that the issue was a problem at the world body but failed to say how many similar cases had been filed so far and how many had been acted upon.
In contrast, it allocated one paragraph to Japan where it said 70 percent of women in a national survey had reported being harasssed sexually, without giving other details.

Some 2,000 officials and activists are attending the Geneva meeting of the world's supreme human rights body which last year churned out 7,000 pages of official documents -- translated, reproduced and distributed -- at a cost of $9 million.
